title: Fourteen years
hookLine: Rama exiled; he accepts in one sentence

cards: Rama wakes up on his coronation morning. The city is decorated for him. The priests are ready.
The water for the ceremony has been gathered from sacred rivers. A messenger comes: your father wants to see you.
Rama walks into Kaikeyi's rooms expecting a blessing, and finds his father on the floor, unable to look at him, unable to speak. Kaikeyi speaks instead. Calmly, she tells him everything.
Bharata will be king. You will go to the forest, dressed as a hermit, for fourteen years. Your father promised.

teach.b: Rama says, in effect: so be it. I'll go. He doesn't argue or bargain.
He tells Kaikeyi he would have given the kingdom to Bharata gladly if anyone had simply asked. His only sorrow is that his father is in pain. Then he walks out.
Valmiki notices one detail, and people have repeated it ever since: Rama's face didn't change. It looked the same when he heard he'd be king, and when he heard he'd be exiled. That isn't coldness.
The people around him are anything but calm. His mother Kausalya is devastated. His brother Lakshmana is furious and ready to fight their father for the throne.
Rama is the steady one, and he talks Lakshmana down. Why does he accept?
Dharma, your third word: doing what's yours to do. For Rama, keeping his father's word is his duty, even when it costs him everything.
That's why tradition calls him maryada purushottam: the ideal person, who keeps within the bounds of right action. Not everyone finds this easy.
Some readers ask whether Rama should have fought, and the tradition lets them ask.
But the scene draws a line worth keeping: giving up and accepting are different. Giving up sits down. Accepting stands up and starts walking.
Rama doesn't pretend it's fair; he just refuses to let the unfairness decide who he is. Hinduism has a whole teaching for this: do what's yours to do, and let go of how it turns out.

how: Many Hindus hold up Rama's acceptance of exile as the model of keeping one's word and duty; the scene is often retold when families talk about hard decisions and honoring parents.

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.

s: Rama argues and bargains to stay
he accepts at once, and says he'd have given Bharata the kingdom gladly.
Valmiki says Rama's face didn't change
the same at the news of crowning and of exile.
the tradition forbids questioning Rama's choice
some readers ask whether he should have fought, and the tradition lets them.

games.q: you're Rama. on your coronation morning, you're told you'll be exiled for fourteen years because of your father's promise. what do you do?
o: accept, and comfort the people around you.
games.why: he accepts in a sentence, talks Lakshmana down, and grieves only for his father's pain.

practice: Think of something in your life that isn't fair and won't change: a diagnosis, a loss, a decision someone else made. Don't argue with it for now; let your face be still, the way Rama's was. Breathe in: this is what is.
Breathe out: what's mine to do next? If you pray, offer the next step to God, the way Rama gave his to dharma.

wordCard.voice: Fourteen years. Rama's exile, accepted in a sentence, on the morning he was meant to be crowned.

orig.note: Sanskrit: forest (vana) dwelling (vasa), the word for Rama's exile.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma, accept, then walk. Even fourteen years begin with one step. That's forty days in.
